title: Café Letter Board
story: A café has a wall board of letter tiles in a grid. On quiz night, teams answer by tracing their word: start on any tile, then slide to the tile directly above, below, left or right for each next letter. No diagonals, and no tile twice in one word.
The quiz host needs a quick check that an answer can really be traced on tonight's board.
task: Write canTrace(board, word). board is a list of equal-length strings, one per row, so board[r][c] is the letter in row r, column c. Return true if word can be traced as described, and false otherwise.
Consecutive letters must be on tiles that share a side, and each tile can be used at most once per word.
constraints: 1 ≤ number of rows, number of columns ≤ 6
board and word contain only uppercase letters A to Z.

examples.explanation:
The board is
C A T
O R E
W E B
Start on C (top left), then down to O, right to R, right to E.
B touches both Es, but the two Es (row 1, column 2 and row 2, column 1) touch only diagonally, so you can never step from one to the other.
R, A, R would need the only R tile twice.

hints: On the example board, CORE can only start on the C. Standing on C, where can the O be?
The next letter must be on one of at most four side neighbours, and the one after must neighbour that tile. A path fails the moment a letter is wrong; then you go back and try another neighbour.

Write trace(r, c, k): can the word from letter k on be traced starting at tile (r, c)? It fails if the tile is off the board, already used, or the wrong letter. It succeeds if k is the last letter. Otherwise ask the four neighbours with k + 1.
Mark the tile used before asking the neighbours and unmark it afterwards, whatever they answered. Call trace(r, c, 0) from every tile and return true if any call does.
bruteForce: From every tile, follow every walk of the word's length (up to four choices per step) and compare letters at the end. On a 6 × 6 board with a 15-letter word that is 36 × 414, around 9.7 billion walks.
Almost all go wrong by the second or third letter. Check each letter as you step on it and turn back at once on a mismatch.

js: * @return {boolean} true if word can be traced
py: def can_trace(board: list[str], word: str) -> bool:

tests.note: a failed first try must free its tiles
one tile cannot be used twice
one letter longer than the board
all letters present, but no T next to an A
the second S is not next to the D
a decoy N next to the O

js: // can word[k..] be traced starting at tile (r, c)?
if (r < 0 || c < 0 || r >= rows || c >= cols) return false;
if (k === word.length - 1) return true; // last letter matched
const found = trace(r - 1, c, k + 1) || trace(r + 1, c, k + 1) ||
trace(r, c - 1, k + 1) || trace(r, c + 1, k + 1);
used[r][c] = false; // free the tile for other paths
py: # can word[k:] be traced starting at tile (r, c)?
if r < 0 or c < 0 or r >= rows or c >= cols:
found = (trace(r - 1, c, k + 1) or trace(r + 1, c, k + 1) or
trace(r, c - 1, k + 1) or trace(r, c + 1, k + 1))
used[r][c] = False                  # free the tile for other paths
return any(trace(r, c, 0) for r in range(rows) for c in range(cols))
walkthrough: Depth-first search with backtracking follows one path as far as the letters match, and steps back to try another neighbour the moment one fails.
• Tiles other than C fail at once on the first letter. At C (row 0, column 0), mark it and look for O among its neighbours.
• Right is A: wrong letter. Down is O: match. Mark it and look for R.
• From O: up is C, already used. Down is W: wrong. Right is R: match. Mark it and look for E.
• From R: up is A, wrong. Down is E (row 2, column 1): it is the last letter, so return true all the way up.

The unmark step matters. On a board like SEA / ETT / ESA with the word TASTE, a first attempt can mark a T, an A and an S and then fail. If they stay marked, they block the correct path, and you wrongly return false.
solution.timeWhy: From each of the R · C tiles, a path of length L branches at most 4 ways at the first step and 3 after that (it cannot go back to the tile it came from). Wrong letters cut most branches early.
solution.spaceWhy: The used grid, plus a recursion stack as deep as the word is long.
solution.takeaway: Grid backtracking: mark a cell on the way in, explore the neighbours, unmark it on the way out. Check the cheap rules (in bounds, right letter, not used) first so dead paths stop after one step.
